title: Kirpan: the small sword
hook: a small sword, carried as a duty to protect the defenseless

segments.voice: Yesterday, kachhera, the K no one sees. Your line was ready and restrained. Did you keep your one quiet restraint? Today, the fifth K, the most misunderstood, and the one that needs the most care to explain. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

Imagine being told: carry this with you always, and hope you never, ever need it. Not a phone or a first-aid kit, but a blade, worn in a cloth sheath across the body, often small, often under the clothes. Most people who hear this for the first time get nervous. Sikhs who carry it often say the opposite: it makes them calmer, because of what it stands for, and the promise attached to it. Today, the fifth of the five Ks: kirpan.
screen: `CARRY IT ALWAYS.` → `HOPE NEVER TO NEED IT.` → `THE FIFTH K.`

segments.voice: The kirpan is a small sword, worn in a sheath on a cloth strap called a gatra, by Sikhs who have taken amrit. The old word simply means sword. But Sikhs love to hear two words inside it: kirpa, mercy or grace, and aan, honor or dignity. That's today's line: mercy and honor. Whatever the linguists say, it tells you what the kirpan is for. It stands for a duty, not a threat: to protect the defenseless, to stand against injustice, as Kabir's true warrior did, the one who fights for the helpless and never leaves the field. Why a sword at all? Remember the history. The Sikh Gurus lived through persecution. Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur were executed by the authorities of their day. Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa as saint-soldiers: saints first, soldiers when they must be. In his letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, known as the Zafarnama, he wrote, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means, first. Sikh teaching is firm that the kirpan is never for aggression, revenge or show; drawing it in anger betrays everything it means. Most Sikhs will go their whole lives without ever drawing it. In many countries, laws make room for it as an article of faith, and Sikhs often wear small or blunt ones, secured in the gatra. It's carried the way the kara is worn: as a reminder. Of mercy. Of honor. Of the people you'd stand in front of.
screen: `KIRPAN — THE SMALL SWORD.` · `KIRPA + AAN: MERCY AND HONOR.` · `SAINTS FIRST, SOLDIERS WHEN THEY MUST.` · `EVERY OTHER MEANS, FIRST.` · then, large: `MERCY AND HONOR.`

segments.voice: Think about whom you would protect. Start with the obvious: a child, a parent, a friend. Then go wider: a neighbor who lives alone, a coworker who gets picked on, someone in your town without a voice. Picture standing beside them, not with a weapon, but with steadiness and care. Ask yourself what protecting them would actually look like this week. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Kirpan. The small sword, the fifth K: carried as a duty to protect the defenseless, and heard by Sikhs as mercy and honor.
Your line: mercy and honor. Today, think whom you'd protect, and do one small thing that stands beside them. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs carry a kirpan at all times in a gatra, often small and worn under clothing, as an article of faith and a reminder of the duty to protect others; Sikh teaching forbids using it in aggression.

fork.setup: someone asks you why a peaceful faith has a sword among its five Ks. what's the answer from today?
options: a duty to protect the defenseless: saints first, soldiers only when every other means has failed.
fork.reveal: the kirpan is a reminder of mercy and honor, and of the people you'd stand in front of.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirpan, the small sword; Sikhs hear kirpa (mercy) and aan (honor) inside it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious weapon.
what it means: a reminder carried always, of mercy, honor and the duty to protect the defenseless, never to be drawn in anger.
what a scholar hears: kirpan derives from Sanskrit kṛpāṇa, 'sword'; the kirpa + aan reading is a popular devotional etymology; Zafarnama (Persian, c. 1705) justifies the sword only as a last resort.
